title: Public Finance Basics
summary: Learn how governments raise and spend money: reasons for public spending, revenue and tax-to-GDP, fiscal policy and multipliers, deficits and debt sustainability, public financial management and procurement, and accountability.
audience: Economics and public-administration students, civil servants, journalists and active citizens

lessons.title: Why governments raise and spend money

body.p: Public finance studies how governments raise revenue, spend it, borrow and manage public resources. Markets do many things well but fail in some areas, which is a main reason for government activity.

list: Public goods: services nobody can be excluded from, such as national defence, street lighting and disease surveillance, which markets under-provide.
Externalities: pollution harms others (a negative externality), while vaccination and education benefit others (positive externalities).
Merit goods: services such as basic education and health that society wants everyone to have.
Redistribution and social protection: grants, pensions and support for vulnerable people.
Stabilisation: managing the economy through recessions and booms.
Infrastructure: roads, water, power and ports that support growth.

body.p: Government can also fail: through waste, corruption, poor targeting or projects chosen for political rather than economic reasons. Good public finance aims for spending that is efficient, effective, fair and accountable.

body.tip: When judging a public programme, ask what problem it solves, who benefits, who pays, and what evidence shows it works.

body.p: Governments raise money mainly through taxes, but also through fees, royalties from natural resources, profits of state companies, grants from donors and borrowing.

A common measure is tax revenue as a share of gross domestic product (GDP). If a country collects 300 billion in taxes and its GDP is 1500 billion, the tax-to-GDP ratio is 300 / 1500 = 20%. Many African countries collect well below the levels of richer economies, partly because of large informal sectors, exemptions and weak collection.

list: Personal and company income taxes.
VAT and other consumption taxes, usually the largest and most stable source.
Customs and excise duties.
Natural-resource revenues, which can be large but volatile with commodity prices.
Local revenues such as property rates and business licences.

body.p: Widening the tax base (bringing more people and businesses into the system and cutting unjustified exemptions) is usually fairer and more efficient than raising rates on those who already pay.

body.tip: Look up your country's budget documents; most finance ministries publish revenue and spending tables each year.

body.p: Government spending is usually divided into recurrent spending (salaries, goods and services, interest, transfers) and capital spending (roads, schools, hospitals, equipment). Capital spending builds future capacity, but is often the first to be cut when money is short.

Fiscal policy uses spending and taxation to influence the economy. In a recession, governments may spend more or cut taxes to support demand (expansionary policy); in an overheating economy they may do the opposite. The simple Keynesian multiplier is 1 / (1 - MPC), where MPC is the marginal propensity to consume. With MPC = 0.8 the multiplier is 5, so 10 billion of extra spending could, in this simple model, raise output by up to 50 billion. Real multipliers are smaller because of taxes, imports and other leakages.

list: Automatic stabilisers: tax revenues fall and unemployment support rises in downturns without new decisions.
Discretionary policy: deliberate new measures, which take time to agree and implement.
Value for money: spending should achieve the most outcome per unit of money (economy, efficiency and effectiveness).

body.tip: Ask whether a spending increase is temporary (for a downturn) or permanent (needing permanent revenue).

body.p: A budget deficit occurs when spending exceeds revenue in a year; it is financed by borrowing, which adds to public debt. If revenue is 300 billion and spending 330 billion, the deficit is 30 billion, 2% of a 1500-billion GDP.

list: Debt-to-GDP: debt of 900 billion in an economy with GDP of 1500 billion is 60% of GDP.
Interest burden: at an average interest rate of 10%, interest costs 90 billion a year, or 30% of the 300-billion revenue, money not available for services.
Foreign-currency debt adds exchange-rate risk: if the local currency falls, the debt grows in local terms.

body.p: Whether debt is sustainable depends on interest rates, growth and the primary balance (revenue minus non-interest spending). When the interest rate exceeds the growth rate, the government needs a primary surplus just to stop the debt ratio rising. With debt at 60% of GDP, an interest rate of 10% and nominal growth of 8%, the required primary surplus is about (0.10 - 0.08) / 1.08 x 60, roughly 1.1% of GDP.

body.tip: Borrowing to build productive infrastructure can pay for itself; borrowing to pay salaries usually cannot.

body.p: Public financial management (PFM) covers the whole budget cycle: planning and preparing the budget, approval by parliament, execution (spending and collecting money), accounting and reporting, and audit and oversight.

list: Medium-term budget frameworks linking annual budgets to longer-term plans.
Treasury single accounts that consolidate government cash for better control.
Commitment controls so agencies cannot spend beyond approved budgets.
Integrated financial management information systems that record transactions.
Timely in-year reports and annual financial statements.
Independent external audit by the Auditor-General or supreme audit institution.

body.p: Governments spend large shares of budgets buying goods, works and services. Procurement laws require competition, transparency and value for money: open tenders, clear evaluation criteria, conflict-of-interest declarations and published contract awards. Weak procurement is a major route for corruption, inflated prices and poor-quality work.

body.tip: Public contracts in many countries are published online; journalists and citizens use them to track how money is spent.

body.p: Citizens pay for government, so they have a right to know how money is raised and spent. Transparency means publishing budgets, reports, audits and contracts in accessible forms; accountability means officials must explain decisions and face consequences for misuse.

list: Parliament approves budgets and scrutinises spending through committees such as public accounts committees.
Supreme audit institutions audit government accounts and report publicly.
Anti-corruption agencies, courts and the media investigate abuse.
Civil society organisations analyse budgets and track service delivery.
Citizens' budgets explain the budget in simple language.

body.p: Many countries share revenue and responsibilities with regional and local governments, such as counties in Kenya, states in Nigeria and provinces and municipalities in South Africa. Decentralisation can bring services closer to people, but needs clear assignment of responsibilities, fair transfer formulas, local revenue capacity and strong local accountability.

body.tip: Read your local government's budget and annual report; participatory budgeting meetings are a direct way to influence local priorities.
